questions.prompt: What best defines the inertia default in this chapter?
choices: Wanting more rest after a busy week
Letting the familiar path continue because changing it feels costly
Reacting emotionally before you have time to think

explanation.gentle: The chapter is not mainly about rest or emotion. It is about familiar continuation gaining automatic authority.
explanation.direct: Inertia appears when a known pattern keeps deciding because interruption feels too expensive.
explanation.competitive: The old path keeps the seat.

questions.prompt: Why can the familiar path feel safer than it really is?
choices: Because familiarity can get mistaken for evidence that the pattern is wise
Because anything familiar is usually the best option
Because the chapter says change is always reckless

explanation.gentle: Knowing a pattern well can make it feel more justified than it truly is.
explanation.direct: Familiarity can borrow credibility it has not earned.

questions.prompt: What is the chapter's clearest warning about weak pattern carryover?
choices: It only matters when people are visibly unmotivated
It can keep wasting time and shrinking options while still feeling stable
It proves that routine is usually harmful

explanation.gentle: The danger is quiet drift, not only obvious failure.
explanation.direct: A bad pattern can survive in respectable form while still reducing flexibility and quality.
explanation.competitive: Drift can look tidy while it closes the field.

questions.prompt: Iris keeps an outdated workflow because rebuilding it would disrupt the week. What chapter principle is most visible?
choices: Reset friction is protecting a weak process
All structure should be abandoned immediately
The problem is mainly social pressure from the group

explanation.gentle: The current process survives because the interruption cost feels too vivid.
explanation.direct: Iris is overvaluing the front-loaded reset pain and undervaluing ongoing drift.
explanation.competitive: The restart fee is keeping the bad system employed.

questions.prompt: Mateo's team knows its handoff system is weak but delays the migration again. According to the chapter, what is happening?
choices: The team is wisely respecting any long-standing system
Familiarity is making the bad process feel safer than the concentrated pain of change
The team is mostly reacting from ego and status defense

explanation.gentle: The known system feels easier to preserve than to interrupt, even though it keeps costing them.
explanation.direct: Inertia is active because reset pain is winning against the accumulated drift bill.
explanation.competitive: The migration hurts first, so the weak tool keeps its badge.

questions.prompt: Keisha keeps the same study routine even though it is not helping much. What response best matches the chapter?
choices: Keep the whole routine because consistency always beats change
Scrap every routine because familiarity is always dangerous
Keep the useful parts but deliberately test a change in the weak segment

explanation.gentle: The chapter preserves useful stability while challenging what survives only as habit.
explanation.direct: The right move is not blind loyalty or total disruption, but examined redesign.
explanation.competitive: Do not worship the whole system. Replace the dead part.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the chapter's difference between stability and stagnation?
choices: Stability avoids all change, while stagnation welcomes it
Stability can still serve the outcome, while stagnation survives mainly because it is familiar
They are basically the same once a routine lasts long enough

explanation.gentle: A useful routine can still deserve loyalty. A stagnant one depends on unexamined continuation.
explanation.direct: The test is whether the pattern still works, not whether it has history.

questions.prompt: Why does reset friction matter so much in the inertia default?
choices: Because the immediate hassle of change can hide the larger long-term cost of staying put
Because any discomfort is proof that the current routine is best
Because the chapter says people should never interrupt a running system

explanation.gentle: The short-term cost of change can feel bigger than the slower cost of drift.
explanation.direct: Front-loaded pain distorts judgment if it makes continuation look cheaper than it is.
explanation.competitive: The visible restart fee can hide months of quiet loss.

questions.prompt: How does Chapter 5 prepare the move into Chapter 6?
choices: By showing that once inertia is named, weak patterns disappear on their own
By showing that better judgment requires building a stronger default, not only criticizing the old one
By arguing that clarity depends on removing all routines from life

explanation.gentle: The next chapter matters because noticing inertia is not enough to replace it.
explanation.direct: Chapter 6 turns diagnosis into design by making clearer thinking more deliberate and repeatable.
explanation.competitive: You do not beat drift with complaint. You install a better system.

questions.prompt: Which question best tests whether staying the course is discipline or comfort in disguise?
choices: Would I choose this same pattern again if it were not already underway?
How long has this routine existed?
Does this pattern feel easier than trying something else?

explanation.gentle: The chapter restores the routine to a choice by asking whether it still deserves renewal.
explanation.direct: Current usefulness matters more than age or ease.
explanation.competitive: Rebuild it or stop pretending it is earned.
